job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Wei Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Wei, and thank you for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in software engineering at Lakeford, and I live in the flat above my family's noodle restaurant with my parents and my little brother. I wake up at seven, fold dumpling wrappers with my mum for an hour, then go to class. After lectures I work on my thesis, a booking system that helps small restaurants handle walk-ins, and I serve the dinner rush on Fridays. My bachelor's was software engineering, with an internship at a payments company and another at an insurance firm. What wears me out is that everyone thinks coding is a lonely job, when mine includes carrying soup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected, and I'd keep working. At the restaurant, I'd say we use the software that makes the bookings easier, nothing more. To friends I'd say good, there's still plenty to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my plan carries on. I finish the master's, take a job as a developer at a decent company, and help my family with their systems. My parents have worked sixteen hours a day for twenty years, and I want to make their life easier, not riskier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my thesis, apply to a dozen companies and pick the steadiest. I'd carry on working Fridays at the restaurant, because it's family. And I'd save to help my parents fix the kitchen ventilation, which they've been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Things stay the same, and the same is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools for your studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, for boring things like test cases. I check everything, because it makes up library names. I'm not against it, I just wait until my classmates have found the problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still worries you if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' health, and the rent on the restaurant. The landlord put it up twice in three years, and one more rise could close us. That's the real risk, and no software fixes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful and not panic. At the restaurant I'd say a booking tool that talks to customers could help, but let's try it on a quiet week. To friends I'd say learn to check the machine's work, since that's the new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it hits the entry-level coding market, which is what I'm training for. Writing, checking and testing code are exactly the thinking tasks that move to software, so companies hire fewer juniors. I'd still be okay, but I'd need to be better than the average graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI tools more, in a steady way, and finish my thesis with the booking system working. I'd target companies in payments and insurance, where they need careful people, not fast ones. And I'd keep helping the restaurant with bookings, as a kind of living portfolio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared, but I'm tired of being told everything is about to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does being careful look like in a job interview?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a project where the machine wrote the first draft and I caught three bugs. Employers want someone who can say no to a bad answer. That's a skill I learned from watching my father reject a delivery of bad fish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whom do you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Jun, a very quick coder who skips testing. In a world where the machine writes fast, being quick is cheap, and being careful is what's left. I told him, and he laughed, but I think he knows.

I'd need to be **better** than the average graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a disaster for the ordinary person and we need to slow down. I'd tell my family and friends to stay close and share what we have. And I'd say the government should speak plainly, because people get scared by silence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened for my career. If thinking AI does almost any desk job by 2028, a software graduate has nothing that makes the first hire. The restaurant is hands-on, so robots for kitchens are 3 years off, but I'm not sure a restaurant makes enough to feed all of us if I earn nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the long-term plan and take any developer job I could, even for less. I'd work extra at the restaurant, and learn the supply and ordering side so I'm useful there too. And I'd save every penny I earn, because if things go wrong, we'll need cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It feels like carrying a full tray across a wet floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the family do if your income doesn't come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We tighten. My parents already don't take much. We'd cut the delivery service, and I'd move into my brother's room so we could rent out mine, which I know sounds silly, but we've done it before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum, I'll work the restaurant every day if I have to, and I'll still look for a job. My mum would say, don't throw your degree away, and I'd say I won't. And she'd put more noodles in my bowl, which is how she says it's all right.

say: I'd say it's a **disaster** for ordinary people and we need to slow down.
I'd tell the family to **stay close** and share what we have.
think: A software graduate has **nothing** that makes the first hire if thinking AI does desk work by 2028.
The restaurant makes enough **only if** I'm earning too.

**Save** every penny and learn the supply and ordering side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something about it, and we shouldn't wait for a crisis. I'd say we should help small businesses adopt tools safely, not leave them behind. And I'd say my restaurant is a good example of one that needs help, not a lecture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel nervous but have a path. By 2031 I'd be 29, with five years of developer experience, and I'd probably be married. The danger is that desk work disappears before I'm established, and hands-on kitchens last until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work in payments or insurance for three years, and then think about building tools for small family businesses. I'd save a third of my salary for my parents' retirement. And I'd marry, I'd say, and buy a flat near the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the sort of thing that makes me plan a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the five-year version different from two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can prepare properly, which is a relief. With two years I'd run home to the restaurant, but with five I can build experience first and still help my parents later. That makes it easier to accept the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to marry and buy a flat, with that date looming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd say so. I'd just keep the flat small and the mortgage smaller. A man with a family needs something to come home to, even if his job changes. I'd rather do it in the order my parents did.

I'd say small businesses need **help**, not a lecture.

The danger is desk work vanishing before I'm **established**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the sensible thing is to carry on and be ready. I'd say don't throw out the old ways just because there's a new one. And I'd say the world has always had people who panic too early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine mostly. By 2036 I'd be 34, with a family and a career, and maybe my own small software business serving restaurants. I'd still be a little uneasy that I'd be competing with a machine that doesn't tire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work for a few years, and slowly build a small business serving restaurants. I'd use the new tools when others have tried them, not before. And I'd save and help my brother go through university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mildly. A decade is long enough to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's seventeen and wants to study design. I'd pay part of his fees, and I'd tell him to take something that needs taste, not just skill. A machine can follow a recipe, but my mother's dumplings are better because she tastes as she goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself, if you could, ten years ago?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to cook properly, and learn to talk to customers. Everything I've learned in the restaurant has been worth more than I expected, and I'd tell the younger me to pay attention.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one, no question. My parents have no spare room for a mistake, and I'm the one who's meant to bring something in. What would help is time, plain advice, and some support for small family businesses like ours, since the rent and wages are tight already. If the government said clearly what happens to rent and wages, that alone would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really, except that I don't say it much, but I'm scared of letting my family down. I plan and save because it's the way I show care. If you write one thing, please write that the people who feed us, like my parents, will have a harder time than the engineers.
